summary: In this episode, Fr. Andrew Stephen Damick and Fr. Stephen De Young discuss the methodology of reading the Bible, contrasting pre-modern and modern approaches to history. They argue that pre-modern history was a purposeful narrative woven from Scripture, extrabiblical literature, and classics, serving to form a people's identity. The modern shift, influenced by 19th-century German academia, treats history as a science (Wissenschaft) and the Bible as evidence, leading to the modernist-fundamentalist debate. Both sides share a flawed presupposition: the Bible makes objective truth claims. The hosts propose reading forward from the Old Testament through the New Testament to the Fathers, seeing Scripture as a growing organism (using Hegel's analogy). Meaning is not a single essence behind the text but is encountered in application—God's energies working through Scripture in the liturgical life of the Church. The episode concludes with practical steps: apply Scripture to oneself first, then to those under one's spiritual care, and encounter Christ through obedience and acts of mercy.

entities.title: George Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
entities.summary: 19th-century German philosopher; the hosts say something nice about him for introducing organic development of concepts through history, used as an analogy for Scripture.

entities.title: Aristotle
entities.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher who said history is a matter of doxa (opinion), not episteme (demonstrable knowledge).

entities.title: Thomas Aquinas
entities.summary: Medieval theologian who used Aristotle's epistemology to argue theology is a science (episteme), not opinion.

entities.title: Donatists
entities.summary: 4th-century North African Christian sect that restricted salvation to their group; Fathers applied 1 John 2:2 to refute them.

entities.title: Marcian
entities.summary: Early heretic who rejected the Old Testament; the hosts note many Christians are functionally Marcianists.

concepts.title: Pre-Modern History
concepts.summary: History as a purposeful narrative woven from Scripture, extrabiblical literature, and classics to form a people's identity, not an objective account.

concepts.title: Modernist History (Wissenschaft)
concepts.summary: History as a science (Wissenschaft) that treats the Bible as evidence to be weighed objectively, leading to a pretense of objectivity.

concepts.title: Reading Forward
concepts.summary: A methodology of reading the Old Testament first, then the New Testament, then the Fathers, seeing Scripture as an organic growth culminating in Christ.

concepts.title: Essence vs. Energy in Scripture
concepts.summary: Applying the theological distinction between God's essence and energies to Scripture: meaning is encountered in God's action through the text, not as a static essence.

concepts.title: Application vs. Interpretation
concepts.summary: The Fathers apply Scripture to their context rather than extracting a single meaning; application is a form of participation in God's work.

claims.text: The Bible is not a modern history book making objective truth claims; it is a story of a people to which you are invited to belong.
Both liberal and conservative biblical scholarship share the modernist presupposition that the Bible makes truth claims that must be verified.
The meaning of Scripture is not a single essence behind the text but is encountered in God's action through the text, applied in the liturgical life of the Church.
The Church Fathers do not interpret Scripture to find a single meaning; they apply it to their context, participating in God's work.
Encountering Christ comes through obedience to His commandments and acts of mercy, not merely intellectual study.

scriptural_links.summary: Cited as the purpose of Scripture: that we may believe and have life in Christ's name.
Used as a test case for reading forward: how first readers would have understood the Nephilim.
Discussed in relation to Matthew 1:23; the original context is the Syro-Ephraimite war, not a prediction of virgin birth.
Matthew applies Isaiah 7:14 to Christ's birth, not as a prediction but as a fulfillment that echoes the original deliverance.
Christ died for the whole world; Fathers applied this to refute Donatists who restricted salvation.

glossary.definition: German for 'science'; in 19th-century German academia, the idea that history should be a scientific discipline.
Greek for 'opinion' or 'glory'; Aristotle said history is a matter of doxa, not episteme.
Greek for 'knowledge' that can be demonstrated, like mathematics; contrasted with doxa.
Greek for 'mindset' or 'way of thinking'; the patristic mindset for reading Scripture.
Latin for 'consensus of the Fathers'; the idea that the Fathers' collective interpretation gives the meaning of Scripture.
